chapters.title: About this manual
chapters.content:
This user manual describes the operation and handling of the Phadia E2000 instrument and its associated software.

This manual is not country-specific and may refer to methods or assays that are not approved for use in certain regions. For country-specific regulatory information, contact your local Thermo Fisher Scientific representative.

Users must complete Thermo Fisher Scientific training before operating the instrument.

chapters.title: System components and software
chapters.content:
The Phadia E system includes:

  • Instrument platform Phadia E2000 and embedded instrument software

  • Phadia E Operator Software

All system components are identified by name. The embedded instrument software and Phadia E are version-controlled. The system is designed to meet defined hardware, IT infrastructure, and cybersecurity requirements, including measures for controlled access and secure operation.

chapters.title: Principles of operation
chapters.content:
The system uses enzyme-based immunoassay technology with fluorescent detection.

Automated processes include:

  • Sample handling

  • Reagent dispensing

  • Incubation and washing

  • Measurement and result calculation

Software functions include:

  • Workflow management

  • Result calculation and reporting

  • Quality control

  • Reflex testing

  • Inventory management

The system supports LIS/LAS connectivity and optional connection to Phadia™ LabCommunity.

Further details on assay principles are provided in the relevant sections:

  • Process overview

  • Specifications

chapters.title: Overview of functionality
chapters.content:
Phadia E instruments are fully automated in vitro diagnostic (IVD) systems designed for use exclusively with ImmunoCAP™ and EliA™ assays manufactured by Thermo Fisher Scientific.

The system is a closed analytical platform. Only manufacturer-specified reagents, calibrators, and consumables can be used. Use of third-party components is not supported and may affect performance, safety, and regulatory compliance.

The instrument performs automated sample and reagent handling, including incubation, washing, fluorescence-based measurement. The instrument allows continuous random-access loading of reagents and samples during runs.

The system may be used as a stand-alone unit, combined with other Phadia E systems, Laboratory Information System (LIS), or integrated with Laboratory Automation Systems (LAS).

chapters.title: Instrument performance and characteristics
chapters.content:
Detailed specifications are provided in the Specification chapter.

Performance characteristics defined for the system include:

  • Handling precision: precision and repeatability of sample and reagent handling

  • Sample throughput: sample processing capacity within a defined time period

  • Temperature control: maintenance of specified operating temperatures within defined limits

  • Measuring range and linearity: defined analytical range and linear measurement

  • Carryover control: measures to minimize carryover between samples and reagents

Device characteristics:

  • Automation: fully automated system operation

  • Measurement type: fluorescence-based analytical measurement

  • Target population: defined according to the intended use of the specific assay

  • Use environment: intended for use in clinical and research laboratory settings

chapters.title: General intended use
chapters.content:
Phadia E instruments are intended for the measurement of analytes in human biological samples, including blood, serum, and stool, using validated ImmunoCAP and EliA methodologies.

The system supports diagnostic applications including:

  • Evaluation of diseases or medical conditions in combination with other clinical findings

  • Assessment of disease status or treatment response over time

  • Evaluation of immune-related activity based on assay-specific analytes

The system is intended for use in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements and only with approved reagents, methods, and components. Deviations from specified use may affect system performance.

In accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR), the device is intended to provide qualitative, semi-quantitative, or quantitative assay-dependent results to support clinical decision-making.

chapters.title: Preparation for instrument service visits
chapters.content:
Prior to a service visit, the operator shall prepare the instrument in accordance with the instructions provided in this manual. Preparation includes, but is not limited to:

  • Performing decontamination procedures, if necessary

  • Ensuring sufficient clearance and access space around the instrument for service activities

Detailed instructions are provided in a service checklist included in this manual.

chapters.title: General warnings
chapters.content:
Use the instrument only as described in the user documentation.

Only trained personnel must use and maintain the instrument.

Use only original parts, accessories, and external equipment, such as USB sticks, barcode scanners, keyboards etc., supplied or recommended by Thermo Fisher Scientific.

chapters.title: Personal protection
chapters.content:
Follow all precautions for handling blood derivatives. Refer to local or national laboratory safety guidelines.

Wear disposable gloves, safety goggles, and a laboratory coat when handling samples or any parts that have been in contact with samples.

Wear disposable gloves, safety goggles, and a laboratory coat when handling reagents.

The liquid waste bottles contain biohazard waste. Avoid direct contact with the liquids and wear disposable gloves when handling the bottles

The biohazard waste bin contains materials that may be infected. Avoid direct contact with the materials and wear disposable gloves when handling the bin.

Dispose of waste materials carefully and according to hazardous waste procedures.

Phadia Maintenance Solution and sodium hypochlorite are classified as hazardous substances. Wear safety goggles, disposable gloves, and a laboratory coat when working with these solutions. See the respective IfU for more information.

chapters.title: Installing and moving the instrument
chapters.content:
The instrument must be installed by a Thermo Fisher Scientific representative and in accordance with the installation guide and local regulations.

Contact a Thermo Fisher Scientific representative if you need to move the instrument. Do not move the instrument yourself.

chapters.title: Power supply
chapters.content:
The instrument must be connected to a properly grounded mains power outlet. Before connecting the power cord, verify that the wall outlet voltage corresponds to the specified operating voltage of the instrument.

Use only grounded power cords supplied or approved by Thermo Fisher Scientific. Replace a damaged power cord only with the same type of grounded cord approved by Thermo Fisher Scientific.

Replace fuses only with the same type and rating as specified for the instrument.

Do not use the device near strong electromagnetic radiation sources, such as unshielded radio frequency sources, as they may interfere with proper operation.

chapters.title: Operation
chapters.content:
Do not use glass tubes or glass vials in the instrument.

Handle sample trays using both hands to minimize the risk of spills.

Take care to avoid hand injuries when both sample drawers are open simultaneously. Opening both drawers at the same time may also increase the risk of cross-contamination between samples.

Do not use consumables beyond their expiration date.

Always remove caps or sample seals from the sample tubes before loading them into the instrument.

Use only sample tubes that meet the specifications defined in the user documentation. Non-compliant tubes may cause incorrect results, mechanical malfunction, or contamination.

Do not pool reagents, as this may cause contamination.

Do not touch or remove the sealing foil on cartridges, as this may cause contamination.

Handle cartridges with care. Do not drop. Dropping may cause damage or rupture and may introduce air bubbles that affect system performance.

Inspecting dropped cartridge

If a cartridge is dropped, inspect it carefully to ensure it is undamaged. Do not use any cartridge that has fallen from a height exceeding the limits specified below, as it may have sustained hidden damage.

  • With primary packaging: 28 cm

  • With secondary packaging: 90 cm

Do not use damaged cartridges. Remove and discard any damaged cartridges immediately.

Wear disposable gloves when handling dilution plates. Do not touch the top surface of the dilution plate, as this may cause contamination.

Discard damaged or contaminated dilution plates immediately.

Do not reuse dilution plates, as this may lead to erroneous results.

Store dilution plates in the original package. Re-seal the package immediately after opening to prevent contamination of dilution wells.

Do not open bottled reagents until required to avoid contamination.

Do not let the bottle connectors come into contact with potentially contaminated surfaces.

Avoid twisting or squeezing the bottle tubing, as this may lead to blockage or worn tubing.

chapters.title: Maintenance and service
chapters.content:
All service and maintenance, except for the procedures described in the user documentation, must be performed by an authorized Thermo Fisher Scientific representative.

Wear disposable gloves, safety goggles, and a laboratory coat when performing manual maintenance tasks, as the inside of the instrument may be contaminated by biohazardous material.

Do not attempt to repair internal instrument components.

Before opening the hood, position the instrument screen so that the moving hood cannot come into contact with or damage the screen.

Perform maintenance as described in the user documentation to ensure safe operation. Failure to perform required maintenance may result in microbial growth and biofilm in the system and its containers.

chapters.title: Biochemical safety
chapters.content:
When operating the Phadia E system, reagents manufactured from human blood components are frequently used. The source materials have been tested for the following and found to be negative:

  • hepatitis B surface antigen

  • antibodies to HIV 1 and HIV 2

  • hepatitis C virus

chapters.title: Risk of infection
chapters.content:
The Phadia E instrument processes human body fluids that may be infectious. When using or maintaining the instrument, avoid touching any parts that have been in contact with samples.

Infectious material from serum or plasma can be transferred to a person in three different ways:

  • Through cuts or punctures from contaminated sharp objects, like a pipette tip.

  • By contact with injured skin or skin affected by eczema.

  • Through airborne particles reaching the mouth or eyes.

Infectious material on healthy, intact skin is not dangerous, but it should be cleaned off quickly to prevent it from spreading to sensitive areas like the eyes, mouth, or damaged skin.

chapters.title: Diseases of concern
chapters.content:
Contagious diseases are caused by infectious agents such as bacteria, parasites, and viruses. In laboratory work with human body fluids, some are more concerning than others. The three most important are:

Virus

Risk of infection

Risk of progression into chronic disease after infection

Hepatitis B virus

As high as 30% when inoculated with blood (serum and plasma) from a highly contagious person. The risk from direct contact or airborne exposure is unknown. Hepatitis B can survive for a long time outside the body, even in dried blood.

Approximately 5%.

Hepatitis C virus

About 2–5% when inoculated with blood (serum and plasma). The risk from direct contact or airborne exposure is unknown.

Between 60 to 90% depending on strain and recipient.

Human immunodeficiency virus, HIV

Depends on the virus count in the infected blood. After inoculation, the risk is about 0.2–0.4%. The risk from direct contact or airborne exposure is much lower. HIV does not survive long outside the body.

Close to 100%. If left untreated, the chronic stage will develop into the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, AIDS.

chapters.title: Infection prevention
chapters.content:
Sample tubes contain serum, plasma or human stool, which can contaminate the work area when loaded into the instrument. Handle anything that may have been in contact with sample materials carefully and follow good laboratory practice.

During operation, the instrument transfers sample material via pipettes from the sample tubes into the caps and wells in the process core. Waste materials collected in the biohazard waste bin and the liquid waste bottles must be handled and disposed of as hazardous waste.

To reduce infection risk:

  • Always wear disposable gloves. Discard the gloves according to hazardous waste procedures.

  • Wash your hands before leaving the lab and before eating.

chapters.title: After contact with serum or plasma
chapters.content:
If serum or plasma touches your skin or mucous membranes, wash immediately with plenty of soap and water. Disinfect with 70% ethanol if possible. Use an eye shower to rinse the eyes.

If you think you may have been contaminated, contact a physician for further advice.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.content:
A sample ID is used to identify a sample in the system. The sample ID can be read from a sample tube barcode and is used in communication with the Laboratory Information System (LIS) for test orders and result reporting.

This section describes how sample IDs and sample tube barcodes are managed in the Phadia E instrument and software.

Different options for sample ID handling are available by pressing More > Settings > Samples > Special sample handling.

chapters.title: Multiple sample tubes for a single sample
chapters.content:
For large test panels, if one sample tube does not provide enough volume for all requested tests, the sample may be divided into multiple tubes. The tubes can then either share the same barcode or have distinct barcodes:

  • Multiple tubes using the same barcode and sample ID: All tubes retain the original barcode.

  • Multiple tubes using the same sample ID with different barcodes: Each tube receives a unique barcode by adding a prefix to the original sample ID, enabling individual tube tracking

chapters.title: Sample tubes with identical barcodes
chapters.content:
A sample can be aliquoted into multiple tubes that share the same sample ID and barcode. In this case, the total sample volume is divided and distributed among the aliquot tubes.

Before assay start, the volume of each sample tube is measured by the instrument. Only tests supported by the available volume in each tube are started.

The LIS must be updated to support multiple sample tubes with the same sample ID.

Enable sample tubes with the same sample ID

Step

Action

1

Go to More > Settings > Samples > Special sample handling.

2

Select Allow sample tubes with same sample id.

Enable sample volume measurement

Step

Action

1

Go to More > Settings > Samples > Tube types and press the relevant tube type.

2

Select Volume calculation.

Run samples with different pre-dilution factors

Running tests with different pre-dilution factors is possible by creating an additional sample with a new sample ID and a different dilution factor. The additional sample uses the same request ID as the original sample, allowing the results to be reported together. This approach can be used when insufficient sample volume requires part of the sample to be transferred to another tube and processed using a different dilution factor.

chapters.title: Sample tubes with different barcodes
chapters.content:
When a sample is aliquoted into multiple tubes that share the same sample ID but must be tracked individually, an additional unique identifier is required to distinguish each tube.

To ensure clear identification, a prefix can be added to the barcode of each aliquoted tube. The barcode structure may include:

  • The sample ID

  • An optional unique identifier for each individual tube

Enable multiple samples with the same ID and different barcode

Step

2

chapters.content:

  • Sample tray ID and position received from LIS

These methods cannot be used at the same time.

chapters.title: Reusing a sample ID for a new sample
chapters.content:
Some laboratories reuse sample IDs. When reuse of sample IDs is enabled, a sample ID is considered unique only within a defined time period. After that period has passed, the same sample ID may be reused for a different sample and request.

To clearly distinguish between reused sample IDs, a time-period identifier is added to the sample ID. Format: YYMM_sampleID

  • Sample ID “12345” run in January 2024 → 2401_12345

  • The same sample ID used in February → 2402_12345

Action

1

chapters.title: Barcode masking
chapters.content:

chapters.title: Troubleshooting introduction
chapters.content:
This section provides guidance for identifying and resolving common instrument and software issues that may occur during operation. Follow Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) and perform only the corrective actions described in this section.

Good Laboratory Practices

  • Respond to fatal and alarm errors immediately.

  • Review error details before taking corrective action.

  • Acknowledge errors and information messages after review.

  • Monitor the Error list task card regularly.

  • Record troubleshooting activities and corrective actions according to laboratory procedures, when required.

  • Report recurring or unresolved errors to Thermo Fisher Scientific Technical Support

When to contact Thermo Fisher Scientific Technical Support

Contact an authorized Thermo Fisher Scientific service representative if:

  • The issue is not described in this manual.

  • An internal, sensor, calibration, voltage/power, fan, or temperature sensor error occurs.

  • A reported error cannot be resolved using the recommended corrective actions.

  • A critical error message is displayed.

  • Instrument safety, functionality, or performance may be compromised.

  • Internal components appear damaged or malfunctioning.

  • Fluid leakage, unusual odors, smoke, or abnormal sounds are observed.

Do not attempt to repair internal instrument components.

Documentation and logging

Document all troubleshooting activities and corrective actions according to your laboratory's standard operating procedures (SOPs). Where applicable, record the following information:

  • Instrument serial number

  • Date and time of occurrence

  • Corrective actions performed

  • Troubleshooting outcome

chapters.title: Assay principle
chapters.content:
The ImmunoCAP and EliA assays are fluoroenzyme immunoassays in which specific antibodies or antigens are covalently immobilized on a highly porous solid matrix for ImmunoCAP or on the walls of the test well for EliA. Upon addition of the sample, the target analyte binds to the immobilized capture reagent. After a washing step, an enzyme-labeled detection antibody or antigen (conjugate) is added to form a specific immune complex.

A second washing step is performed to remove any unbound conjugate. Subsequently, a fluorogenic substrate is added. The enzyme associated with the conjugate converts the substrate into a fluorescent product. After the reaction is stopped, the fluorescence intensity is measured. The fluorescence signal is directly proportional to the concentration of the target analyte in the sample .

The responses obtained for patient samples are converted to concentrations using a calibration curve for result evaluation.

chapters.title: ImmunoCAP assay timeline
chapters.content: The assay requires 94 minutes to complete.

chapters.title: Detailed process
chapters.content:
The test is transferred from its carrier to the immunoreaction wheel (IRW).

The storage buffer and any released allergens or antibodies are removed from the test. All liquid is then aspirated from the test.

Patient samples, calibrators, curve controls, or quality controls are aspirated from their sample tubes or cartridges. If required, the samples are diluted before being dispensed into the test.

Target analytes bind to antigens or antibodies in the test.

Unbound proteins are removed through washing and aspiration.

Conjugate is aspirated from cartridges and dispensed into the test.

Conjugate antibodies bind to analytes attached to the solid phase.

Excess unbound conjugate is removed through washing.

The test is moved to the enzyme reaction wheel (ERW).

Development solution is dispensed into the test.

The conjugate reacts with the non-fluorescent substrate and fluorescent product is generated.

Stop solution stops the enzyme reaction and elutes fluorescent product.

Fluorescent product is eluted through the bottom of the test into an elution well.

Eluate is transferred to the fluorometer and the fluorescence is measured.

Used tests are removed from the ERW and discarded into waste.

The elution wells are rinsed to prevent carry-over contamination before reuse.

chapters.title: EliA assay timeline
chapters.content: The assay requires 94 minutes to complete.

chapters.title: Detailed process
chapters.content:
The test is transferred from its carrier to the immunoreaction wheel (IRW).

Patient samples, calibrators, curve controls, or quality controls are aspirated from their sample tubes or cartridges. The samples are diluted before being dispensed into the test.

Target analytes bind to antigens or antibodies in the test.

Unbound proteins are removed through washing and aspiration.

Conjugate is aspirated from cartridges and dispensed into the test.

Conjugate antibodies bind to analytes attached to the inner surface of the EliA well.

Excess unbound conjugate is removed through washing.

The test is moved to the enzyme reaction wheel (ERW).

Development solution is dispensed into the test.

The conjugate reacts with the non-fluorescent substrate and fluorescent product is generated.

Stop solution stops the enzyme reaction.

Eluate is transferred to the fluorometer and the fluorescence is measured.

Used tests are removed from the ERW and discarded into waste.

chapters.title: Sample process
chapters.content:
Step

Description

1

The operator loads a sample tray with samples in one of the sample drawers and closes the drawer.

2

The sample tray is scanned by the instrument to identify the tray ID and which tube positions are filled.

3

Each sample tube is lifted and scanned to detect the sample ID and the separation between the layers in the tube. The state of the scanned samples changes from Not started to In progress.

4

The sample tubes are either moved to the instrument’s internal sample storage or returned to the sample drawer if the internal sample storage is full.

5

When it is time for pipetting the samples are transferred to the sample shuttle, which moves to the pipetting position.

6

The samples are pipetted and diluted if needed. The sample state changes to Pipetted.

7

The samples are returned to a sample tray in a sample drawer. Samples for reflex testing are held in the internal sample storage if there is available space, otherwise they are returned to a sample tray.

8

The relevant ImmunoCAP or EliA tests are fetched from carriers in the internal reagent storage and dispensed in the process core.

9

The sample is dispensed into the cap or well.

chapters.title: Process core
chapters.content:
The assay process takes place in the process core in the center of the instrument deck. The process core consists of a process bowl and a process chamber lid. The rotating process bowl transports the tests to the modules in the non-rotating process chamber lid where the different sub-steps of the assay process take place. chapters.title: Process bowl
chapters.content:
The process bowl contains the immunoreaction wheel (IRW) in the center and the enzyme reaction wheel (ERW) surrounding it. Both wheels have holes in rows and spokes. The IRW has 78 spokes and 4 rows, and the ERW has 90 spokes and 2 rows. The outermost row on each wheel is designated as row number 1.

The IRW rotates counterclockwise one position every minute and takes 78 minutes to complete a full revolution. The ERW rotates clockwise one position every 30 seconds and takes 45 minutes to complete a full revolution.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.content:
The instrument has two independently accessible sample drawers (1) for loading trays with sample tubes. A total of 400 tubes can be loaded in the sample drawers. The drawers must be unlocked before they can be opened.

Each drawer has four sample tray positions (2). The tray positions in the sample drawer are designed so the tray can only be inserted in one orientation. Position A1 on the tray is always located in the inner left corner (3) of the tray position.

The sample drawers can be configured to use both drawers as input and output, or to use the left drawer as input and the right drawer as output.

The sample drawers lock when they are closed, and the contents of the sample trays are scanned.

chapters.title: Sample trays
chapters.content:
Handle sample trays using both hands to minimize the risk of spills.

Sample tubes are placed in washable sample trays. Sample trays are not restricted to a specific instrument and can be shared between different Phadia E instruments within a laboratory.

Each sample tray has 50 tube positions.

A spring in each tube position allows the use of different tube sizes. The springs can be replaced when needed.

Each sample tray should have a sticker with a unique tray ID. The sticker is applied by the laboratory and can be replaced when needed.

chapters.title: Internal sample storage and sample shuttles
chapters.content:
After scanning, samples can either be kept in the sample drawers or moved to an internal sample storage, or to one of two sample shuttles used for transporting tubes to pipetting. This is done by the instrument and not controlled by the user.

The internal sample storage has 40 tube positions. Each sample shuttle has 20 tube positions.

[add images]

Samples that have been moved to the internal storage or the sample shuttles are not shown on the Samples page or the Trays page. They can be viewed and unloaded by searching for the sample ID in the search field or on the Requests page.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.content:
Reagents are loaded in the reagent drawer (1). The drawer must be unlocked before it can be opened.

The reagent drawer has four positions for dilution plates at the back (2) and four positions for reagent loaders at the front (3). The dilution plates are placed in stacks of five in each position. Cartridges and carriers can be placed together in any order in a reagent loader.

The content of the reagent drawer is scanned each time the drawer is opened and closed again. No position information is kept from previous scans.

If the drawer is not closed within 5 minutes you are asked to close the drawer. The drawer locks when it is closed.

chapters.title: Reagent loaders
chapters.content: A reagent loader is a container for both cartridges and carriers. Each reagent loader can hold 12 cartridges, 72 carriers or a combination of carriers and cartridges. Reagent loaders have no identifiers and can be placed in any empty position in the reagent drawer.

Do not pool reagents, as this may cause contamination.

Cartridges have a foil seal on top with a 2D code positioned in two corners. A piercing tool breaks the foil when a cell needs to be opened. The 2D code lets the instrument keep track of which cells have been pierced. Pierced cells are considered empty and cannot be reused if a cartridge is reloaded.

Do not touch or remove the sealing foil on cartridges, as this may cause contamination.

There is also a label wrapped around the sides of the cartridge with a UDI code that is scanned by the instrument.

Cartridges must be stored with the sealing foil facing upwards, otherwise air can gather at the bottom of the cartridge cells. Avoid humid conditions, as they may cause condensation to form on the sealing foil. See the respective cartridge label or Instruction for Use for recommended storage temperatures.

chapters.title: Carriers
chapters.content:
Carriers contain ImmunoCAP or EliA tests. ImmunoCAP carriers are color-coded by method, all EliA carriers are beige. Carriers can be put in the reagent loader with or without caps. Caps are automatically removed by the instrument.

Carriers are labeled on the top with the short name of the test. The label on the side of the carrier contains a UDI code that lets the instrument keep track of the number of remaining doses in a carrier.

chapters.title: Dilution plates
chapters.content:
Dilution plates are loaded in the back of the reagent drawer. Each of the four loading positions can hold a stack of up to five plates. It is recommended to load a full stack of five plates whenever a position is empty. This ensures that plates do not remain in the instrument for long periods of time.

Store dilution plates in the original package. Re-seal the package immediately after opening to prevent contamination of dilution wells.

The bottle drawer has color-coded positions that correspond to the colors on the bottle labels.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.content:
The liquid drawer (1) contains both the rinse solution (purified water) and the liquid waste. The drawer is unlocked and can be opened at any time.

The liquid waste bottles contain biohazard waste. Avoid direct contact with the liquids and wear disposable gloves when handling the bottles

The liquid drawer contains four bottles that can contain 5–10 liters each: two bottles for rinse solution (2) and two bottles for liquid waste (3). The liquid drawer has color-coded positions that correspond to the colors on the bottle labels and caps. The instrument automatically detects if bottles are present in the drawer.

chapters.title: Bottle connectors
chapters.content:
Each rinse and waste bottle has two caps. One is a plain cap (1) used to empty or refill the bottle. The other cap has two quick connectors (2) for the liquid flow to the instrument. During use, both connectors must remain attached to the bottle, including during manual rinse and waste operations.

The two connectors on the cap have different sizes to facilitate correct connection. The smaller connector is used for inflow to the bottle, and the larger connector is used for outflow from the bottle.

The bottle is connected by pressing the top part of each connector into the bottom part until it clicks into place.

The bottle is disconnected by pressing the release button on each connector and pulling the connectors upwards.

chapters.title: Piped-in rinse and piped-out waste
chapters.content:
The rinse solution is supplied from either a laboratory piped-in rinse tube or the onboard rinse bottles.

The instrument can dispose of liquid waste through the piped-out waste tube or collect it in the onboard waste bottles.

When piped-in rinse and piped-out waste are enabled, handling of rinse and waste is automatic. Only one bottle of each type is used in the liquid drawer, as a temporary buffer for the liquids. The arrows show inflow and outflow of liquid in the bottles.

chapters.title: Manual rinse and waste
chapters.content:
If the laboratory does not have piped-in rinse and piped-out waste lines, rinse and waste is handled in the onboard bottles. The bottles must be refilled and emptied manually.

A task card is shown if a waste bottle needs to be emptied or a rinse bottle needs to be refilled. During assay processing one bottle can be emptied or refilled while the other bottle is in use.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.content:
Solid waste is handled in the waste drawer (1). The drawer must be unlocked before it can be opened.

The biohazard waste bin contains materials that may be infected. Avoid direct contact with the materials and wear disposable gloves when handling the bin.

The waste drawer contains two waste bins:

  • The inner bin is used for biohazard solid waste (2).

  • The outer bin is used for recyclable solid waste (3).

It is recommended to use a plastic bag in each waste bin to reduce the risk of contamination. The plastic bag must have a minimum size of L × B × H cm. If the bag is too small the waste level may be read incorrectly by the sensor.

Biohazard solid waste includes carriers and cartridges with remaining tests, used caps and wells, and dilution plates. Recyclable solid waste includes carrier caps. The laboratory can configure whether cartridges and carriers shall be disposed of as biohazard or recyclable waste. Disposal requirements may vary according to local regulations and laboratory procedures. This flexibility helps reduce the amount of biohazard waste and related disposal costs.

Expired and empty cartridges and carriers are automatically discarded to waste. If the waste drawer is opened during an assay, cartridges and dilution plates are kept in the instrument until it is possible to discard them. Used caps and wells are kept in the waste chute for up to 10 minutes of processing. A task card prompts the operator to close the drawer before the waste chute is full. After 10 minutes the instrument stops dispensing tests until the drawer is closed and the bins are detected again.

If the waste level in either bin reaches the defined upper limit, the instrument pauses test dispensing. A task card informs the operator that the waste bin must be emptied.

chapters.title: Waste chute
chapters.content: The waste chute (1) is positioned inside the instrument, behind the internal front cartridge storage and to the left of the reagent drawer. It directs solid waste into the waste bins: the small opening directs waste to the outer bin, while the large opening directs waste to the inner bin. The waste chute is magnetically attached to the instrument and can easily be removed for cleaning.

chapters.content:
Carriers and cartridges are loaded into the instrument in the reagent drawer, then transferred to the instrument’s internal reagent storage. Dilution plates are loaded in the reagent drawer and kept there until needed, when they are transferred to the internal dilution plate positions. Bottled reagents are loaded and stored in the bottle drawer. All products stored in the internal storage areas are listed on the Inventory page on the instrument screen.
